the spread of smoking can be modelled by a three-population compartmental model with multiple linearly frequency-dependent peer influence.

the introduction of generalised peer incidence into the three-population smoking model can lead to a tipping-point dynamic, and that the presence of systemic uncertainty in the model can lead to the tipping-point occurring at a lower level of smoking prevalence than would otherwise be the case.
multiple peer influence can affect the stability of steady-state smoking levels, and introduce a new kind of dynamic, which can be described by a tipping point.

the development and application of a novel mathematical framework for the investigation of the social spread of smoking.

the spread of smoking is not only affected by the number of smokers in the population, but also by how many people have stopped and are trying to remain non-smokers.
